messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
We need about 175 m with a 60 g raw egg, and the flight time window is 55-60 s. Motors are limited to H or smaller. It usually blows around 3 m/s at our field. Cheers.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 175 m, so within 5%, about 166 to 184 m. Payload is a raw egg of 60 g, which is 0.060 kg, a minimum mass that has to fly. Flight time is a window of 55 to 60 s, a range, not a single target. Motor class is a maximum of H. Wind is about 3 m/s, and I will pass that on every flight. Rail is not stated, so 1.5 m. Vertical, sea level, single stage, one parachute. The long flight from a low apogee means a slow chute, not a big motor.
2. Feasibility: 175 m with no drag needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 175) = 59 m/s. Descent has to fill most of a 57 s flight, so the sink rate wants to be near 175 / 50 = 3.5 m/s. A C or a D can reach 175 m once the egg is aboard; an H would overshoot badly. Looking up a C and a D.

2. Feasibility: the D12 is 16.8 N*s, 10.4 N average, 24 mm, delays to 7 s, class D, under the H cap. The C6 is only 4.8 N. With a 0.060 kg egg the liftoff mass is near 0.20 kg, and 4.8 / (0.20 * 9.81) = 2.45, under the 3:1 gate, so the C6 cannot lift this. The D12 can. A long flight from 175 m is a chute problem: 175 / 50 = 3.5 m/s average sink if the coast is a few seconds and the rest of a 57 s flight is descent.
3. Size: thrust-to-weight on the D12 is 10.4 / (0.20 * 9.81) = 5.30. Rail acceleration (10.4 - 1.96) / 0.20 = 42.2 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 42.2 * 1.5) = 11.2 m/s on average thrust. The D12 spikes to 29.7 N, so the real exit should clear 15 m/s. Descent mass 0.20 - 0.021 = 0.179 kg. At 3.4 m/s and Cd 0.8, area = 2 * 0.179 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 3.4^2) = 0.310 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.310 / 3.1416) = 0.628 m. I will fit a 0.65 m chute. Burn is 1.61 s, so the 7 s delay ejects near 9 s.
4. Draft: 54 mm cardboard tube, long enough for an egg, short ogive, three balsa fins, 24 mm mount, D12-7, 0.060 kg mass named as the raw egg payload, 0.65 m chute on ejection. Wind 3 m/s.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: the simulator gives 172.6 m, and (175 - 172.6) / 175 = 0.0137, about 1% under 175 m, inside the 5% band. Flight time is 50.0 s, below the 55 s floor of the window. The chute opens at 8.7 s, and 8.7 - 6.33 = 2.4 s after apogee, so the rocket free-falls and the tool warns of deployment at 22.2 m/s. That free-fall is why the flight is short: landing rate once the chute is open is 3.5 m/s, which is slow enough. Rail exit 17.1 m/s, thrust-to-weight 4.7, margin 1.26 cal. The egg is aboard. Wind was 3 m/s.
5. Fix: 50.0 s is the miss. The 7 s delay is late. Changing it to 5 s puts ejection at about 1.61 + 5 = 6.6 s, next to apogee at 6.33 s. The coast then happens under the chute instead of in free-fall, which should add the missing seconds and kill the 22.2 m/s opening. Altitude should stay near 172 m. Nothing else changes.

4. Check: the simulator gives 55.6 s. That sits inside the 55 to 60 s window, 55.6 - 55 = 0.6 s above the floor. Apogee is still 172.6 m, and (175 - 172.6) / 175 = 0.0137, inside 5%. The chute now opens at 6.7 s, just after apogee at 6.33 s, at 5.5 m/s, and the high-speed warning is gone. Landing 3.5 m/s is under 6. Rail exit 17.1 m/s, thrust-to-weight 4.7, margin 1.26 cal. Motor is a D12, under the H cap. The 0.06 kg egg is in the tube. Wind was 3 m/s.
5. Fix: no further change; altitude and flight time both pass.
6. Uncertainty: 55.6 s is only 0.6 s above the bottom of the window. A chute that opens a little less fully than Cd 0.8, or a heavier egg, shortens the flight back under 55 s. Apogee at 172.6 m has more room inside the 5% band than the clock does. Drift at 3 m/s was 111 m. The egg is modeled as a point mass of 0.06 kg, not as a fragile shell.
messages.content:
A 54 mm cardboard egg-loft on an Estes D12-5, carrying a 0.06 kg raw egg and a 0.65 m chute.
In a 3 m/s wind the simulator gives 173 m and a 55.6 s flight, inside the 55 to 60 s window, landing at 3.5 m/s.
